content: Corticosteroids are commonly considered for the treatment of sore throat due to their ability to reduce inflammation in the upper respiratory tract. Sore throat is a frequent condition that often leads to high rates of antibiotic prescriptions, despite limited evidence supporting the effectiveness of antibiotics in this context. This review aimed to evaluate the clinical benefits and safety of corticosteroids in alleviating sore throat symptoms in both adults and children. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared corticosteroids to either placebo or standard care in individuals aged over three years with sore throat. Studies involving hospitalized patients, those with infectious mononucleosis, sore throat following tonsillectomy or intubation, or peritonsillar abscess were excluded. A total of nine trials with 1319 participants (369 children and 950 adults) were analyzed. In eight of these trials, participants in both the corticosteroid and placebo groups also received antibiotics, while one trial used a delayed antibiotic prescription approach based on clinical assessment. The findings demonstrated that corticosteroids significantly increased the likelihood of complete pain resolution at 24 hours by 2.4 times (risk ratio [RR] 2.4, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.29 to 4.47) and at 48 hours by 1.5 times (RR 1.50, 95% CI 1.27 to 1.76). These results were supported by high-certainty evidence. To prevent one person from continuing to experience pain at 24 hours, five individuals would need to be treated with corticosteroids. Additionally, corticosteroids reduced the mean time to the onset of pain relief by 6 hours and the mean time to complete pain resolution by 11.6 hours, although there was significant variability in these results. Pain, as measured by visual analogue scales, was reduced by an additional 10.6% at 24 hours with corticosteroids. No significant differences were observed between corticosteroids and placebo in terms of recurrence or relapse rates, days missed from work or school, or adverse events. However, the reporting of adverse events was limited, and only two trials included children or reported data on days missed from work or school. The overall quality of the evidence was assessed as moderate, but the small number of included studies introduces some uncertainty, particularly regarding the applicability of these findings to children. In conclusion, oral or intramuscular corticosteroids, when used alongside antibiotics, moderately increased the likelihood of pain resolution and improvement in individuals with sore throat. Despite these benefits, the limited magnitude of the effect highlights the need for further research to better understand the potential harms and benefits of short courses of corticosteroids, enabling more informed clinical decision-making.
